findings.evidence: Statement: represent α- and β-decay by a radioactive decay equation of the form ${}^{238}_{92}U \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}Th + {}^{4}_{2}\alpha$; item 9702-11.1-i112 asks, 'How do β− and β+ change $Z$?'
findings.suggested: Add a question requiring students to write a complete β-decay equation with the daughter nuclide and emitted particles.
findings.resolution: fix: Finding valid: recalling changes to Z does not test constructing complete beta-decay equations. Show the nucleon and proton numbers of each daughter nucleus, the emitted electron or positron, and the appropriate (anti)neutrino.", "marks": 4, "rubric": [{"point": "(a) Daughter nucleus is ${}^{14}_{7}N$.", "keywords": [["14"], ["7"], ["N", "nitrogen"]]}, {"point": "(a) Complete equation: ${}^{14}_{6}C\\rightarrow{}^{14}_{7}N+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\\bar\\nu_e$. Accept β− for the electron and an explicitly named electron antineutrino.", "keywords": [["electron", "e", "β−"], ["antineutrino", "bar"]]}, {"point": "(b) Daughter nucleus is ${}^{18}_{8}O$.", "keywords": [["18"], ["8"], ["O", "oxygen"]]}, {"point": "(b) Complete equation: ${}^{18}_{9}F\\rightarrow{}^{18}_{8}O+{}^{0}_{+1}e+\\nu_e$. Accept β+ for the positron and an explicitly named electron neutrino.", "keywords": [["positron", "e", "β+"], ["neutrino", "nu"]]}], "explanation": "In β− decay a neutron becomes a proton: $A$ stays 14, $Z$ rises from 6 to 7, and an electron and electron antineutrino are emitted: ${}^{14}_{6}C\\rightarrow{}^{14}_{7}N+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\\bar\\nu_e$. In β+ decay a proton becomes a neutron: $A$ stays 18, $Z$ falls from 9 to 8, and a positron and electron neutrino are emitted: ${}^{18}_{9}F\\rightarrow{}^{18}_{8}O+{}^{0}_{+1}e+\\nu_e$. Charge balances as $6=7-1$ and $9=8+1$; nucleon number is conserved.", "hints": ["Keep the daughter nucleon number equal to the parent nucleon number.", "Balance charge using −1 for an electron and +1 for a positron.", "Include an antineutrino for β− and a neutrino for β+."]}

findings.evidence: Statement: use the unified atomic mass unit (u) as a unit of mass; item 9702-11.1-i122 asks, 'How many kilograms are in $1u$?'
findings.suggested: Add a mass calculation or comparison in which students use u as the mass unit.
findings.resolution: fix: Finding valid: recalling the definition and kg equivalent does not test using u to express a mass. Calculate its mass in u. Use $1\\,\\mathrm{u}=1.66\\times10^{-27}\\,\\mathrm{kg}$. Give your answer to three significant figures.", "marks": 1, "answer": {"value": 4.0, "unit": "u", "sf_ok": [3]}, "explanation": "Divide the mass in kg by the mass of one u: $m=(6.64\\times10^{-27})/(1.66\\times10^{-27})=4.00\\,\\mathrm{u}$.", "hints": ["Express the mass as a number of atomic mass units.", "Divide by the mass in kg of one u.", "Calculate 6.64 ÷ 1.66 and report the result in u to three significant figures."]}
